prompt.context: It is 2003, and our client offers after school programming focused on supporting at-risk youth through high school, enabling them to enter and succeed in college. The client is trying to identify the best approach to meet its growth target. The client's goals for expansion are to most efficiently serve students at 7 new sites, while raising their national profile. We have been hired to help them vet potential sites to maximize their social and financial impact.
prompt.question: What is the best approach for the client to expand to 7 new sites in a way that maximizes social and financial impact while raising its national profile?

clarifying_info.a: 'At-risk' youth are those who, due to behavior or grades, are at risk of dropping out of high school or have already done so.

clarifying_info.q: What does the client's operation look like?
clarifying_info.a: The client operates local centers attached to high schools with full-time staff.

clarifying_info.q: What services does the client provide?
clarifying_info.a: The client offers tutoring and test prep support to the youth with whom it works, as well as connecting youth to internships and career opportunities.

clarifying_info.q: Where does the client currently operate?
clarifying_info.a: All centers are in Massachusetts or southern New Hampshire.

clarifying_info.q: How many sites and students does the client currently serve?
clarifying_info.a: The client operates 8 sites with 2,500 youth served.
School districts and state agencies reimburse the client for activities.

clarifying_info.q: Has the client received interest from other geographies?
clarifying_info.a: The client has a high national profile and has received calls from high school systems in Florida and California offering to pay for the client to establish centers in their districts; the client has declined these offers to date.

exhibits.title: Additional Central Costs from Expansion
exhibits.shows: A table listing current and additional central office cost line items (Staff, IT, Office expenses, Training and support), with rows for Total central office costs and Cost per site left blank for the candidate to calculate.

exhibits.title: Representative Data on At-Risk Youth
exhibits.shows: A table with five columns showing average high school enrollment, annual % change in at-risk youth (2003), number of high schools, HS completion rate (class of 2002), and % of enrolled students with GPA of D or lower for four geographic areas.

framework: Geographic options for new sites: adjacencies to existing sites (neighboring high schools/middle schools), new sites in existing states separate from current sites, neighboring states, or new states that have contacted the client
Methods for opening new sites: partnerships, branching/licensing, wholly-owned sites
Mission-related site selection criteria: number of at-risk youth, presence of other youth service organizations, potential to work with high schools, knowledge of target market

Finance/operations site selection criteria: potential to attract funding, ability to leverage relationships and engage in political advocacy, ability to leverage existing infrastructure, ability to recruit talent

questions.prompt: Question 1: What are the client's options for locating and opening new sites, and what considerations should guide selection among these options?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify three geographic tiers: (1) adjacencies to existing sites (neighboring high schools, middle schools), (2) new sites in existing states separate from current sites, (3) new states (neighboring or those that have contacted the client). Candidate should identify three opening methods: partnerships, branching/licensing, and wholly-owned sites. Candidate should then derive two sets of screening criteria tied back to the client's dual goals of mission and financial impact: mission-related (density of at-risk youth, other youth organizations present, access to high schools, local knowledge) and financial/operational (funding potential, political relationships, existing infrastructure leverage, talent recruitment).

questions.prompt: Question 2: How does expanding to 7 new wholly-owned sites affect the per-site allocation of central office costs? (Show Exhibit 1)
questions.guidance: Candidate should note that the 74% increase in central costs is less than the 88% increase in number of sites (from 8 to 15), so cost per site decreases. Candidate should calculate total new central costs and the new per-site allocation.

math.setup: Current central costs = $1,000K across 8 sites. Additional costs from expansion: Staff +$600K, IT +$80K, Office expenses no change, Training and support +$55K. Total additional = $735K. New total = $1,735K across 15 sites (8 existing + 7 new).
math.answer: New cost per site = $115.67K, down from $125K. The 74% cost increase is smaller than the 88% increase in sites, so central cost allocation per site decreases by ~$9.33K.

questions.prompt: Question 3: Which geographic areas show the most promise for mission fulfillment based on density of at-risk youth? (Show Exhibit 2)
questions.guidance: This is a complex calculation. Candidate must derive total at-risk students in 2003 for each geography using the provided data. High school is 4 years (4 classes at any time). Assume class sizes, dropout rates, and GPA averages are uniform across grades. Worcester neighbors an existing site; Nashua does not. Candidate should work through the formula columns systematically. Worcester and Barrington show highest % of at-risk students; San Mateo has the largest absolute number but lower percentage.

math.setup: Columns: A=Avg enrollment per HS, B=Annual % change in at-risk youth 2003, C=# high schools, D=HS completion rate class of 2002, E=2002 % enrolled with GPA D or lower. Derived columns: F=A*C (total enrollment), G=F/4*(1-D) (dropouts class of 2002), H=G*3 (dropouts other 3 classes), I=G+H (total dropouts), J=F-I (remaining) * E (low GPA students, note: formula is F*E - I*E simplified as (F-I)*E), K=I+J (total at-risk 2002), L=K*(1+B) (total at-risk 2003), M=L/F (% at-risk 2003).
math.answer: % at-risk 2003: Worcester 45.9%, Barrington 44.0%, Nashua 41.6%, San Mateo 32.3%. Worcester has the highest density of at-risk youth. San Mateo has the largest absolute number (1,681) but the lowest density. Worcester and Barrington rank highest on mission fit by density.

questions.prompt: Question 4: What are the pros and cons of the additional screening factors across geographic options? How should this influence target geography selection?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will construct a 2x2 or table matching geographic options (neighboring site, new site in existing state, neighboring state, new state) against mission-fit and financial-fit criteria, then walk through pros and cons for each cell. Key insight: expanding within existing or neighboring states preserves funding model approval, relationship leverage, and operational infrastructure, while new states (like California) offer new funding but carry higher execution risk and the model may not be approved.

questions.prompt: Question 5: Wrap up with a summary and recommendation to the client.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recommend focusing on existing states and possibly neighboring states. Client should not expand outside its New England footprint at this time. Key reasoning: (1) financially, scale benefits apply regardless of geography, but existing states have approved funding models; (2) mission-wise, existing and neighboring geographies (Worcester, Nashua, Barrington) have the highest density of at-risk youth; (3) operational risk is lower in familiar geographies where relationships with policy makers, school admins, and funders already exist.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the pros and cons of expanding to a neighboring site vs. a new state for both mission and financial fit?

categories.name: Neighboring/existing state - Mission
ideas: Pro: deep knowledge of local youth and community needs
Pro: established relationships with policy makers and school administrators
Con: may not spread the model geographically or raise national profile as effectively

categories.name: Neighboring/existing state - Financial
ideas: Pro: funding model already approved by districts/state agencies
Pro: ability to move staff or hire locally with ease
Pro: can leverage existing central infrastructure
Con: may hit funding limits if geographic concentration is too high

categories.name: New state - Mission
ideas: Pro: would spread the model and raise national profile significantly
Con: requires building new relationships from scratch
Con: regulations and school district structures could differ and affect operations

categories.name: New state - Financial
ideas: Pro: access to new sources of funding (new districts and state agencies)
Pro: higher national profile could attract philanthropic donors
Con: districts and states may not fund the model initially
Con: longer ramp time to establish credibility and reimbursement

recommendation: The client should focus expansion on new sites in its existing states (Massachusetts, New Hampshire) and consider neighboring states (e.g., Connecticut), targeting geographies with the highest density of at-risk youth such as Worcester, MA and Barrington, CT

The client should not pursue expansion to distant new states (e.g., California) at this time, despite inbound interest, as the financial and operational risks outweigh the benefits given the client's current scale
risks: Expanding too broadly too quickly could strain central operations and reduce service quality
New state entry risks funding approval delays and regulatory differences that could impair the model
next_steps: Conduct deeper site-level analysis for Worcester, MA and Barrington, CT as primary candidates
Evaluate partnership or branching options in addition to wholly-owned sites to accelerate the 7-site expansion efficiently
Develop a playbook for replicating the funding/reimbursement model in any new state entered
